summary:
Marsivity is a 3D survival simulation where players run a Martian outpost for one full year (668 sols, fast-forwarded). Players keep oxygen, health, rest, food and water alive while balancing habitat power, heat and radiation shielding from a central control panel. They drive a rover across terrain built from NASA MOLA elevation data, place survey flags, collect rock samples and spend them on a research tree. Dust storms, solar flares and freezing nights are driven by Curiosity RAD, REMS and DONKI records, so the dangers follow real patterns. The simulation is accompanied with an optional Arduino powered dashboard that shows the analog reading of energy levels, with knobs controlling radiation shielding, temperature control, and life support. This dashboard immerses players into the decision making process using interactive elements that have real consequences in game. 

It addresses the challenge by turning real engineering trade-offs into decisions a student feels firsthand: dust cuts solar power, less power means less oxygen, and stronger shielding costs energy. A kid-friendly low-poly look and plain-language tooltips keep it fun for young learners, while the real data keeps it honest. It matters because students learn why Mars missions succeed or fail by trying to survive one.
details:
What it does and how it works. Marsivity is a Unity game with a pure C# simulation separate from the visuals. Each sol, the simulation updates power, radiation, weather, farming and the five survival stats. Solar output depends on dust opacity, sun angle and distance from the Sun. Radiation dose depends on the Curiosity RAD background level, flare activity and the shielding the player chooses. Crops grow according to light, water and CO2 values based on NASA Kennedy Space Center plant-growth research. Oxygen comes from tanks refilled by a converter modeled on Perseverance’s MOXIE experiment, which turns Mars’ CO2 into oxygen using power. A daily schedule file built from real mission data tells the game when dust storms, flares and cold nights happen.

The dashboard is powered by an Arduino which sends real time information from the board to the game, such as the position of each knob. The dashboard also outputs in game data such as energy levels to LEDs and an analog gauge for players to engage with.

Benefits. Players see how Mars life support is a web of linked systems. A dust storm is not just a bad-weather event. It reduces power, which slows the oxygen converter and the grow lights, so the player has to decide what to cut.

Intended impact. Make real mission engineering understandable and memorable for students, especially ages 7 to 14, without oversimplifying it. The end-of-year report shows what hurt and what saved the crew. Hands on interaction with a working dashboard also increases engagement with young players.

Tools. Unity with the Universal Render Pipeline, C#, Cinemachine, Input System, Json.NET, and Unity Test Framework. Python (requests, pandas, numpy, Pillow) builds the data files offline, so the game makes no network calls while running. Code is on GitHub. Arduino IDE is also used for connecting the dashboard to the game.

Creativity. The game uses a low-poly sunset look instead of a dull technical interface, a tool-based exploration loop (sweeper, shovel, hammer, camera, radio, wrench), and a research tree driven by samples and survey flags. The radio gives flare warnings with a realistic Earth-Mars light delay.

Factors considered. Age-appropriate language, colorblind-safe indicators, keeping the science credible, and being transparent about data. Where a real data source was unavailable, the pipeline generated seeded synthetic values and labeled them.
dataRefs: Curiosity (MSL) Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD) data, NASA PDS
Curiosity Rover Environmental Monitoring Station (REMS) data, NASA PDS Atmospheres Node
NASA DONKI Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information
Mars Global Surveyor MOLA Gridded Data Records (MEGDR), PDS Geosciences Node
Mars MGS MOLA DEM 463m, USGS Astrogeology
NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, Revision C: Crew Health
Veggie: Space Vegetables for the International Space Station and Beyond (NASA Kennedy Space Center), NTRS
Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment (MOXIE), Hecht et al. 2021, Space Science Reviews
